name: Moxa cupping

lead: Moxa cupping combines two traditional practices: moxibustion, burning dried mugwort near or on the skin, and cupping, applying suction cups. Practitioners say the warmth improves circulation of blood and qi, and some people seek it for muscle relaxation and skin or body-shaping results.

Research on each part is mixed in quality. A 2023 Cochrane review found moderate-certainty evidence for moxibustion in breech presentation, while reviews of cupping report low-to-moderate evidence for musculoskeletal pain that may not differ from placebo.

paras: A practitioner places cups, often glass or bamboo, on the back or other areas while moxa is burned in or near them, or warms cups with the burning herb. Sessions leave round marks that fade over days.

Both parts carry burn and infection risks; cupping causes bruise-like marks and can worsen eczema or psoriasis. Cambodia's health ministry has warned people with high blood pressure or heart problems about cupping.

chain: Suction and warmth applied to the skin
angle.text: Practitioners use warmth and suction to relax muscles and, they say, promote circulation. Appearance benefits are claimed rather than measured.

lead: Moxa cupping refers to using burning moxa, processed mugwort, together with suction cups. It draws on moxibustion, a traditional Chinese medicine therapy also found in Japan, Korea, Vietnam and Mongolia [1], and cupping, which has roots from Iranian and Roman medicine to Chinese practice [2].

Practitioners say moxa warms points to improve circulation of blood and qi, and treats "cold" or "yang deficiency" conditions [1]. Cupping is used for muscle tension and is popular among athletes such as Michael Phelps [2]. People who want smoother-looking skin or relaxed muscles sometimes seek the combination, though the appearance claims are mostly practitioner and user reports.
Research evaluates the two practices separately; no trial of the combination is identified.

paras: Moxibustion burns mugwort directly on the skin, or indirectly via a moxa stick held near it or heated on an acupuncture needle [1]. Fire cupping uses a flame inside the cup to create suction; practitioners may also slide cups with massage oil [2].

Portuguese missionaries in 16th-century Japan were among the first Westerners to describe moxibustion, and Hermann Buschoff's 1674 book popularised the name moxa [1]. The earliest recorded Chinese cupping dates to Ge Hong, 281-341 AD, and Chinese hospitals have used it since the 1950s [2].

No studies found on moxa combined with cupping. Separately, a 2023 Cochrane review found moderate-certainty evidence that moxibustion with usual care may reduce breech presentation, with poorly reported safety [1]. Reviews of cupping report low-to-moderate evidence for musculoskeletal and myofascial pain that may not differ from placebo, and no good evidence for acne [2].

Moxibustion can cause burns and infection, and direct methods can leave scars [1]. Cupping can cause petechiae and purpura, scarring, burns, skin darkening and infection, and may worsen eczema or psoriasis [2].

timeline.event: Earliest recorded Chinese use of cupping, attributed to Ge Hong [2].
Hermann Buschoff's book helps establish the name moxa in English [1].
